title: Useability Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning Toolboxes for Electrical Drives
abstract: The current direction of development predicts that Reinforcement Learning based data driven control methods can become a next generation technology to control electrical drives instead of the classical model-based techniques. The paper aims to evaluate toolboxes that can be used to train agents for control approaches. The paper helps lay the theoretical bases and provides guidelines for using these toolboxes via a case study. This is done to highlight each toolbox’s key aspects and workflow patterns, shifting the comparison to useability and peak-performance. Key words. Artificial Intelligence, Reinforcement Learning, Electrical Machines & Drives, Permanent Magnet Synchronous Machine, Power Electronics

title: Deep generative models for unsupervised anomaly detection in magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
abstract: This thesis explores unsupervised anomaly detection in magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, leveraging generative models to model the distribution of healthy anatomy and identify deviations as anomalies. We examine the integration of additional contextual information into generative models and anomaly scoring methods. Our approaches enhance reconstruction quality and anomaly detection accuracy.

title: A General Framework for Context-Aware Fuzzification of Four Ordered Categories: A Case Study on BMI Categories
abstract: This paper presents a general methodological framework for constructing context-aware fuzzy partitions that extend conventional crisp categorizations. The approach is based on Nov´ak’s theory of fuzzy contexts and is implemented using the R package lfl. It enables smooth and interpretable transitions between adjacent classes while preserving the original categorical structure. To illustrate the procedure, we apply it to derive fitness-specific fuzzy partitions of Body Mass Index, where the conventional four categories (underweight, normal weight, overweight, obese) are adapted according to individual levels of cardiorespiratory fitness.

title: Natural language processing for automatic error detection in Chinese language learning
abstract: With the rapid development of global Chinese language education, the demand for efficient and accurate automated teaching assistance tools is growing.Traditional manual grading methods are often time-consuming and yield inconsistent results, highlighting the necessity for intelligent technological solutions.This paper explores the application of natural language processing techniques in automatic error detection for Chinese as a second language.It proposes a method based on pre-trained language models and evaluates it using a publicly available corpus of Chinese learner compositions.Experimental results demonstrate the strong performance of the proposed method in identifying grammatical and lexical errors, achieving detection accuracy exceeding 80% for major error categories.This represents a significant improvement over baseline systems (over 25% increase).This technology shows great potential as an efficient teaching support tool, enabling more effective and consistent feedback mechanisms within intelligent educational environments.

title: Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons
abstract: Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons is as apt as a title can get. In the initial chapters, Robert Brandom gives us reasons for why one would develop a logic. These reasons are that logic studies and explicates reason relations, the foundational notion in a conception of language as a game of giving and asking for reasons. Ulf Hlobil, in the following chapters, gives us such logic(s) for reasons. In a jointly authored conclusion, Hlobil and Brandom ensure that the pieces fit together. The logic(s) for reasons indeed satisfy the reasons for logic. Hlobil adds an optional epilogue in which he presents a speculative metaphysics, derived from taking as Firsts the most general description of what is postulated by the logic(s) for reasons.Brandom’s chapters are, by themselves, a reason for the philosophical pursuit of rigorous logic as well. Writing against the background of the worked-out logics of the latter chapters visibly aids Brandom’s presentation, highlighting the use of logic to achieve clarity. One finds here the most lucid view yet of Brandomian neopragmatism. Some prior (if passing) familiarity is, however, still needed. The neopragmatist moves are made here with renewed perspicuity but not discussed in the same depth as elsewhere. Readers find a clear picture of what it is to rest a philosophy of language on reason relations but must look elsewhere for objections and responses, for the virtues and vices of this strategy compared to other approaches, or for its intellectual history. Such further discussion would, however, be misplaced in this work. The achievement here is to make the view and its upshots as clear as possible, both in its exposition and in its formalization.These initial chapters elaborate familiar Brandomia that are newly suffused with bilateralia, insights derived and elaborated from the expanding literature on bilateral logic. Reasons can occur as reasons for and as reasons against, so there are reason relations of entailment and of incompatibility. Bilateral logic promises an avenue to spell out such bifurcations and the latter chapters make good on the prospect. Overall, then, this is a happy marriage. It is only in the margins that the Brandomia occasionally rub against the bilateralia. For one, Brandom remains committed to the claim that “the fundamental speech act is that of … asserting” (3), but bilateralists require distinct “fundamental acts” of both “affirmation and denial” (30). This has downstream consequences.The book’s running theme is that logical vocabulary is explicative of more fundamental reason relations. To begin, suppose A is a reason for B. This can be expressed in a formal metavocabulary as A⊢B. However, it may not be possible to express in the object-language that A is a reason for B. Only after expanding the language with a symbol ‘>’ for the conditional, one can express that A⊢B with the object-language sentence ‘A>B’. Thus, having the conditional allows one to accept or reject that A is a reason for B, whereas without it one could only use A as a reason for B. Conversely, A may also be a reason against B, which may be expressed in the metavocabulary as A#B. Brandom’s primacy of asserting is thus about the relata of reason relations in the object-language: potential assertions stand in relations of entailment or incompatibility. Bilateralism provides a bifurcated metalinguistic description of the reason relations themselves.More precisely, Hlobil and Brandom define A⊢B to mean that commitment to accepting A precludes entitlement to reject B, and A#B to mean that commitment to accepting A precludes entitlement to accept B. It is clearest here how new bilateralist talk of acceptance and rejection refines old Brandomian talk of commitment and entitlement. But, oddly, the left-hand side of either definition mentions only acceptances while on the right-hand sides there is once acceptance and once rejection. It seems, however, that commitments to rejections can preclude entitlements just as much as commitments to acceptances. One’s commitment to reject ‘Socrates is speaking’ may preclude entitlement to also reject ‘Socrates is mute’ and preclude entitlement to accept ‘Socrates is orating’. Such relations may well be part of the game of giving and asking for reasons—now understood as involving commitments and entitlements to acceptances and rejections, no longer commitments and entitlements tout court—but cannot be expressed in the proposed metalanguage, at least not literally. That rejecting A precludes also rejecting B is equivalent to ‘⊢A,B’ and that rejecting A precludes accepting B is equivalent to ‘B⊢A’. But these expressions, strictly speaking, describe other rules of the game.Reason relations obtain between sentences but the relations themselves are described in terms of commitments and entitlements to acceptances and rejections. The role of commitments to rejections is absent. So the bilateralism of acceptance and rejection does not seem to map perfectly onto the bifurcation of entailment and incompatibility. Here is another reason to think so. As the conditional makes explicit the turnstile, negation is supposed to make explicit the pound sign. But negation alone is insufficient to express A#B in the object-language, as negation is unary and incompatibility is binary. One requires additional expressive power, conjunction, to say ‘not (A&B)’. So although negation can make explicit (unary) rejection, it cannot by itself make explicit (binary) incompatibility.My even being able to raise such fine-grained complaints is a testament to the clarity and rigor of the presentation here. That they even are complaints is a testament to the ambition of the project. The goal is to be able to make explicit any and all possible reason relations. This ambition is fulfilled to a remarkable degree. The matter of rejective commitments can be tentatively set to the side, as equivalent reason relations are covered.In chapter 3, Hlobil introduces the Non-Monotonic, Multi-Succedent (NMMS) logic. It has the property that for any set of atoms that stand in any configuration of entailment/incompatibility relations (given minimal constraints), each such relation can be expressed by an NMMS sentence. The logic is starkly substructural, so as to avoid making any undue demands on the foundational reason relations. Using a suite of charming examples, it is demonstrated that both entailment and incompatibility could be nonmonotonic and nontransitive. Then, since logical vocabulary is what allows one to explicate a reason relation, logical validity can be construed as whatever is valid regardless of the underlying reason relations. Hlobil demonstrates that these logical validities include the classical validities (consequence is, of course, still substructural). The examples and the results are so compelling that one could easily miss how sophisticated NMMS really is.For one, some operational rules are nonstandard. The usual right-rule for conjunction is to conclude Γ⊢A&B from Γ⊢A and Γ⊢B, but Hlobil adds a third premise, Γ⊢A,B. As before, Γ⊢Δ means that accepting all members of Γ precludes rejecting all members of Δ. Thus, a situation in which the two standard premises hold, but not the added third one, is one in which accepting Γ precludes rejecting A and rejecting B but does not preclude rejecting both. It is initially puzzling how this could be and, so, what work the third premise does. Earlier, Hlobil explains that Γ⊢A is merely a necessary condition for it being proper to accept A based on Γ. Thus, one can extrapolate, it can be that Γ⊢A without it being proper to accept A based on Γ. Then, the desired situation is one in which necessary conditions for the proper acceptance of A and B obtain (Γ⊢A and Γ⊢B), but it is still improper to do so since a necessary condition for accepting either does not obtain (not Γ⊢A,B).Similarly, the left-rule for disjunction lets one infer Γ,A∨B⊢Δ from Γ,A⊢Δ and Γ,B⊢Δ and Γ,A,B⊢Δ. The first two say that, given Γ, accepting A precludes rejecting Δ and accepting B precludes rejecting Δ. One may be inclined to shorten this to say that accepting A or B precludes rejecting Δ, so the third premise may seem superfluous. But, again, two necessary conditions for accepting Δ may obtain (namely, that accepting A precludes rejecting Δ and that accepting B precludes rejecting Δ), but a third necessary condition fails (namely, that accepting both A and B precludes rejecting Δ). For instance, Γ might have consequences not blocked by A and not blocked by B, that are yet blocked by A and B together. Thus, Hlobil logic has a three-legged disjunctive syllogism.These may be counterintuitive readings of the bilateral language. Readers are regularly reminded of the technical definitions, but some examples for the new rules would have helped. It seems that the Nixon Diamond will do for conjunction. That Quakers are pacifists is a necessary condition for properly accepting “Nixon is a dove” based on his religious affiliation; and that Republicans are interventionists is a necessary condition for properly accepting “Nixon is a hawk” based on his party affiliation. Yet it would not be proper to accept either conclusion, since either one is a reason against the other and, so, a necessary condition for accepting either fails. Hlobil’s third premise is therefore not met here and, thus, works to block the bad conclusion that Nixon is both a hawk and a dove. The initial puzzlement is resolved by reading the normative terms themselves as nonmonotonic: it could be precluded to reject A but still proper to reject A and also reject something else.Apprehending this reading is rewarded with a better understanding of how Hlobil and Brandom conceive of reason relations. Based on this understanding, however, some pragmatists may now say that the reason relations are once-removed from language use. There could be reason relations that never show up in the game of giving and asking for reasons since these relations express merely necessary conditions for something whose sufficient conditions are never (and perhaps cannot ever be) fulfilled. Then again, one may also take this to mean that the reason relations are the underlying subject matter of semantics beyond surface use, roughly akin to how representationalists study truth conditions that may never be met. Hlobil and Brandom go some way navigating this dialectic in the remaining chapters.The bilateral normative-pragmatic metavocabulary is merely used for the first formulation of NMMS. Chapter 4 explores the semantic-representational metavocabulary, in which entailment and incompatibility are alethic relations of inclusion and impossibility. This leads to a development of a truth-maker semantics for reason relations—and a natural definition of truth-maker consequence that is isomorphic to NMMS. Hlobil and Brandom note that both the normative-pragmatic and the semantic-representational viewpoints involve conceptual resources that go beyond the mere idea of reason relations. This makes them extrinsic metavocabularies.Thus, although both metavocabularies are about entailment and incompatibility, they do not share a notion of content. Chapter 5, then, presents a third route to NMMS, implication-space models, whose metavocabulary only involves conceptual resources derived from the reason relations themselves (making it intrinsic). This yields a definition of contents as inferential roles that requires nothing more than that the bearers of such contents stand in reason relations. This is a remarkable achievement and a significant contribution to the study of (propositional) contents. To compare: one might think of content as what is truth-apt. But to spell this out, one typically requires a host of additional notions (such as properties or truth-makers). Hlobil and Brandom present a notion of content free from such additions.The formal work is, therefore, deep and significant. Hlobil and Brandom make a conciliatory move in the debate between inferentialists and representationalists. Both approaches, they maintain, are just two ways of talking about one subject matter. Representationalists study reason relations in alethic terms; inferentialists study them in normative terms. This is a striking intervention. Both inferentialists and representationalists can speak of the same contents by using the intrinsic metavocabulary. Previously, given some suitable completeness result, they could at most agree on equivalent consequence relations among very different contents. Hlobil and Brandom thus open an avenue for conciliation also on the metaphysics of meaning.Naturally, this can only go so far. Not all representationalists (nor all inferentialists, for that matter) will agree that their object of study is reason relations. In the end, the pragmatics first order of explanation (the primacy of giving and asking for reasons) remains nonnegotiable to Hlobil and Brandom. One may also wonder whether the conciliation survives conflict. Given two contents, an inferentialist might claim that they are (normatively) incompatible while a representationalist denies that they are (alethically) impossible. A Moore paradox might lead to such a situation, as it is normatively precluded but alethically possible. To resolve disagreement about a common subject matter of reason relations, perhaps either normative or alethic relations must take priority. The authors seem to disagree here. Hlobil’s epilogue contains a derivation of “the world” as setting an alethic standard of correctness. Brandom dissents in an endnote.Besides these grander implications, neopragmatists will also benefit from (finally!) possessing a rigorous notion of content, as some problems related to the former lack of such a notion may now be answerable. For instance, neopragmatists are pressed to say not just what it is to believe or assert some content (or otherwise use it in the game of giving and asking for reasons) but also what it is to hope, fear, or regret that same content. They now have a fighting chance.Reasons for Logic, Logic for Reasons is thus a key achievement in neopragmatism, presenting a long-desired formal treatment of its version of the doctrine. Its formal innovations, especially the notion of content and the conciliatory project it enables, are apt to reshape the debate in semantics. This work improves our understanding not just of meaning but of the study of meaning itself.

title: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis for Interactive Fusion of Dual Perspectives Under Cross-modalInconsistent Perception
authors: BU Yunyang, QI Binting, BU Fanliang
abstract: In social media,people’s comments usually describe a certain sentiment region in the corresponding image,and there is correspondence information between image and text.Most previous multimodal sentiment analysis methods only explore the interactions between images and text from a single perspective,capturing the correspondence between image regions and text words,leading to results that are not optimal.In addition,data on social media is strongly personal and subjective,and the sentiment in the data is multidimensional and complex,which leads to the emergence of data with weak image and text sentiment consistency.To address the above two problems,a multimodal sentiment analysis model with interactive fusion of two perspectives under cross-modal inconsistency perception is proposed.On the one hand,cross-modal interaction of graphic and textual features from both global and local perspectives provides a more comprehensive and accurate sentiment analysis,which improves the perfor-mance and application of the model.On the other hand,the inconsistency scores of the graphical features are calculated to representthe degree of graphical inconsistency,as a way to dynamically regulate the weights of the unimodal and multimodal representations in the final sentiment features,thus improving the robustness of the model.Extensive experiments are conducted on two public datasets,MVSA-Single and MVSA-Multiple,and the results demonstrate the validity and superiority of the proposed multimodal sentiment analysis model compared to the existing baseline models,with F1 values increasing by 0.59 persentage points and 0.39 persentage points,respectively.

title: Uncertainty-Based Streaming ASR With Evidential Deep Learning
abstract: Attention-based encoder-decoder (AED) models achieve high accuracy in offline automatic speech recognition (ASR), but their application to streaming remains challenging due to the lack of mechanisms for regulating token emission. Existing approaches include monotonic attention, forced alignment with external models providing token-level boundaries, and encoder-based emission control methods. However, these methods either require structural modifications, complicate the training pipeline, or show limited accuracy. In addition, local agreement has been proposed as a method enabling streaming without retraining, but it incurs fixed delays corresponding to the input window size and premature commitments. To address these limitations, we propose Evidential Streaming TRAnsformer (ESTRA), a framework that leverages evidential deep learning (EDL) to estimate uncertainty. ESTRA models token probabilities with a Dirichlet distribution and introduces hierarchical and direct Kullback–Leibler divergence losses to ensure uncertainty decreases progressively as more speech is observed. During inference, token emission is controlled by comparing uncertainty against a threshold, suppressing premature outputs without fixed delays. Experiments on the LibriSpeech benchmark show that ESTRA achieves streaming performance comparable to offline AED models, surpasses local agreement in robustness under small input windows, and reduces 50th-percentile latency by avoiding fixed window-size delays, while leaving room for improvement at the 90th percentile. Furthermore, it provides more reliable control of token emission than probability- or entropy-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of uncertainty as an indicator. ESTRA offers a promising approach to streaming ASR, with results supporting the effectiveness of uncertainty-driven token emission.

title: Quantum Optical Integrated Sensing and Communication With Homodyne BPSK Detection
abstract: In this letter, we propose a quantum integrated sensing and communication scheme for a quantum optical link using binary phase-shift keying modulation and homodyne detection. The link operates over a phase-insensitive Gaussian channel with an unknown deterministic phase rotation, where the homodyne receiver jointly carries out symbol detection and phase estimation. We formulate a design problem that minimizes the bit-error rate subject to a Fisher information-based constraint on estimation accuracy. To solve it, we develop an iterative algorithm composed of an inner expectation-maximization loop for joint detection and estimation and an outer loop that adaptively retunes the local oscillator phase. Numerical results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach and demonstrate a fundamental trade-off between communication reliability and sensing accuracy.

title: Strict-tolerant conditional logics
abstract: Abstract We construct a conditional logic using selection models in a three-valued setting. When the selection function selects an empty set, the corresponding conditional is neither true nor false. The semantic consequence is defined as in strict-tolerant logic. The resulting logic validates conditional excluded middle without assuming that a selection function always chooses a single world, reconciling Stalnaker and Lewis. We give a labelled sequent calculus for the logic and consider three extensions of it. With the sequent calculus in hand, we show the decidability of two systems. It turns out that two extensions are strongly connexive, hyperconnexive, superconnexive and almost totally connexive. We compare our logics with other connexive conditional logics and show the philosophical consequence concerning paraconsistency and überconsistency.

title: Solar Energy Potential Prediction Model of Array Office Block Based on Ensemble Learning Algorithm
abstract: In the context of the artificial intelligence era, machine learning algorithms can be used to achieve rapid prediction of the solar potential of urban blocks. However, most of the existing studies used computer simulation, this paper aims to construct a prediction model of the solar potential of urban blocks based on machine learning algorithms. This paper constructs a parametric model of office blocks based on real block cases in Wuhan city, and develops an arrayed solar potential prediction model for office blocks based on ensemble learning algorithms. The results showed that the ensemble learning prediction model can achieve rapid prediction of solar potential, achieve rapid feedback of solar potential of the design scheme, and significantly improve the efficiency of the performance evaluation and design optimisation of the urban block design scheme; the R 2 of the solar potential prediction model for the roof and façade are 0.99 and 0.98, respectively, and the prediction model has a high degree of accuracy. This study aims to provide a decision-making basis for the planning and design of urban office blocks, improve the scientific and rational design, and help urban office blocks achieve carbon neutrality.

title: Overview of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, and Large Language Models
abstract: This chapter provides an overview of the technology underpinning large language models (LLMs). It introduces the historical context of artificial intelligence (AI), from symbolic systems to statistical approaches and deep neural networks, highlighting milestones in natural language processing (NLP). It also addresses the limitations of LLMs, such as hallucinations, biases, and a lack of explainability, and the different types of LLMs according to their information-sharing approaches. The chapter aims to help readers understand LLMs and their underlying algorithms, setting the stage for a deeper exploration of ethical considerations and applications in subsequent sections of the book.

title: When Does Quantum Differential Privacy Compose?
abstract: Composition is a cornerstone of classical differential privacy, enabling strong end-to-end guarantees for complex algorithms through composition theorems (e.g., basic and advanced). In the quantum setting, however, privacy is defined operationally against arbitrary measurements, and classical composition arguments based on scalar privacy-loss random variables no longer apply. As a result, it has remained unclear when meaningful composition guarantees can be obtained for quantum differential privacy (QDP). In this work, we clarify both the limitations and possibilities of composition in the quantum setting. We first show that classical-style composition fails in full generality for POVM-based approximate QDP: even quantum channels that are individually perfectly private can completely lose privacy when combined through correlated joint implementations. We then identify a setting in which clean composition guarantees can be restored. For tensor-product channels acting on product neighboring inputs, we introduce a quantum moments accountant based on an operator-valued notion of privacy loss and a matrix moment-generating function. Although the resulting Rényi-type divergence does not satisfy a data-processing inequality, we prove that controlling its moments suffices to bound measured Rényi divergence, yielding operational privacy guarantees against arbitrary measurements. This leads to advanced-composition-style bounds with the same leading-order behavior as in the classical theory. Our results demonstrate that meaningful composition theorems for quantum differential privacy require carefully articulated structural assumptions on channels, inputs, and adversarial measurements, and provide a principled framework for understanding which classical ideas do and do not extend to the quantum setting.

title: Evolution of Android's Permission-based Security Model and Challenges
abstract: Android Permission Model and Application (app) analysis has consistently remained the focus of the investigation of research groups and stakeholders of the Android ecosystem since it was launched in 2008. Even though the Android smartphone operating system (OS) permission model has evolved significantly from `all-or-none access' to `user-chosen dangerous resource access', specific challenges and issues remain unresolved even after 15 years after the smartphone OS launch. This study addresses the issues and documents the research work in this arena through a comprehensive literature survey and comparative analysis. The survey's focal point is the Android permission model and relevant research between 2010-2022. We systematize the knowledge on (i) Android API Calls to permissions mapping, (ii) Android Permissions evolution, and (iii) how permissions are checked. Furthermore, the survey identifies the permission-related issues and relevant research addressed during the last decade. We reference seminal work in these areas. We summarize the identified research gaps and present future directions for early and experienced researchers.

title: STEP: Success-Rate-Aware Trajectory-Efficient Policy Optimization
abstract: Multi-turn interaction remains challenging for online reinforcement learning.Current GRPObased methods-either at the trajectory level or the step level-still suffer from fundamental challenges in multi-turn settings: they allocate sampling uniformly across tasks regardless of difficulty, propagate misleading learning signals that penalize correct intermediate actions in failed trajectories, and incur high samplecollection costs under long-horizon environments.Step-level variants (e.g., GIGPO) mitigate some interaction-cost constraints by decomposing trajectories, yet they retain GRPO's sampling imbalance and still struggle with heterogeneous multi-turn tasks.To address these issues, we propose STEP (Success-rate-aware Trajectory-Efficient Policy Optimization), a framework that dynamically allocates sampling based on per-task success rates and performs fine-grained step-level optimization.STEP maintains a smoothed success-rate record to guide adaptive trajectory resampling, allocating more effort to harder tasks.It then computes success-rate-weighted advantages and decomposes trajectories into step-level samples, followed by a step-level GRPO augmentation that strengthens updates on low-success tasks.Experiments on OSWorld and AndroidWorld show that STEP substantially improves sample efficiency and training stability over both trajectory-level and existing step-level GRPO variants, converging faster and generalizing better under the same sampling budget.
